title: What is mandatory training?
description: Mandatory training explained: legally required versus organizationally required courses, how to set scope and refresh cycles, and what evidence to keep.
shortAnswer: Mandatory training is training that a person must complete as a condition of their role, either because a law, license or regulator requires the outcome or because the organization has decided it is essential. It is defined by who must complete it and by when, rather than by topic, and it should be justified by a documented requirement or risk so that the list stays short and defensible.
keyTakeaways: Mandatory training has two sources: external requirements (law, license, regulator, standard, contract) and internal decisions (policy or risk).
Most laws require a training outcome, such as workers being trained to work safely, rather than a named course.
Some roles need formal training and assessment before they start, for example operating high risk equipment.
Every mandatory item should record its source requirement, the roles in scope, the refresh trigger and the evidence required.
Mandatory training is a superset of most compliance training, but the two terms are not identical.

blocks.text: Mandatory training is any learning that people in a defined role must complete, with consequences if they do not. The label describes an obligation to participate, not a subject area.

It helps to separate two categories. **Externally required** training traces to a law, regulator rule, license condition, accreditation standard or contract. **Internally required** training is set by the organization to manage a risk or support a policy, even where no external rule names it. Both are legitimate. The difference matters when deciding what can be removed, shortened or delivered in a different format, because only internal requirements are fully within the organization's control.
In health care the phrase "statutory and mandatory training" is common: statutory items come from legislation, and mandatory items come from the employer or a professional or accreditation body.

sections.heading: Where do mandatory training requirements come from?

blocks.text: Most external requirements set an outcome that training must achieve. In the European Union, Article 12 of the [OSH Framework Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31989L0391) requires every employer to ensure each worker receives adequate safety and health training specific to their workstation or job, on recruitment, on a change of job, and when new equipment or technology is introduced. Portugal applies this through [Law 102/2009](/regulations/portugal-ohs-training-requirements).

Some rules are more prescriptive about the training itself. In the United States, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard for powered industrial trucks, [29 CFR 1910.178(l)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.178), requires the employer to ensure each operator "is competent to operate a powered industrial truck safely, as demonstrated by the successful completion of the training and evaluation specified in this paragraph (l)", before the operator is permitted to operate one. Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act similarly requires special education before a worker is assigned designated dangerous or harmful work ([details](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training)).

sections.heading: How does mandatory training differ from compliance training?

blocks.text: Mandatory training describes who must complete something. [Compliance training](/glossary/compliance-training) describes why: to meet a compliance obligation. Most compliance training is mandatory for the roles it covers, but mandatory training can also include items with no compliance purpose, such as an induction to a new system.

Mandatory training is also different from [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency). Completing a mandatory module records participation; verification checks that a person can actually perform the task. Rosters of mandatory items are usually managed in a [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix), which maps each role to its required items.

sections.heading: What should a defensible mandatory training list record?

blocks.text: A mandatory item is defensible when anyone can see why it exists, who it applies to and how completion is proven. The checklist below is an original template for reviewing each item.

items: **Source requirement:** the law, clause, regulator guide, contract term or internal policy, with a link.
**Roles in scope:** named roles, not "all staff" by default.
**Learning outcome:** what the person must be able to do afterward.
**Evidence:** completion only, assessment, or observed competence.
**Timing:** before starting the task, within a set period of starting, or on a refresh cycle.
**Refresh trigger:** a fixed interval, and also any change to the source requirement or process.
**Owner:** the person accountable for the content and its currency.

blocks.title: Illustrative example
blocks.text: A logistics business reviews 22 mandatory items against this checklist. Items without a source requirement or risk rationale are reclassified as optional, and two items covering the same safety obligation are merged. The result is a shorter list in which every remaining item can be explained to an auditor. The numbers are illustrative.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry holds the source requirement for each learning outcome as structured data, so a mandatory item carries its reason with it. When a requirement changes, the affected outcomes and assessments can be identified before learners are reassigned.

faqs.q: Can an organization make any training mandatory?
faqs.a: Yes. Employers can require training that is reasonably connected to the role and to lawful directions. It is good practice to record the reason for each internal requirement so that the list does not grow without review, and to consult on changes where workplace agreements or consultation duties apply.

faqs.q: How often should mandatory training be repeated?
faqs.a: Follow any interval set by a license, standard or regulator first. Otherwise set a risk based interval and also refresh when the underlying requirement, process or risk changes. The guide on [mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) covers this in detail.

faqs.q: What happens if staff do not complete mandatory training?
faqs.a: Consequences depend on the source. For externally required training, the organization may be unable to show it met a legal duty, and the person may be unable to perform the task lawfully. For internal items, consequences are set by policy, for example restricted system access until completion.

faqs.q: Does mandatory training have to be e-learning?
faqs.a: No. Training can mix formal and informal processes, including on the job training, demonstration and feedback. The format should suit the risk and the learning outcome, and higher risk tasks usually need practical assessment.
